question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\frac{1x}{5}$. Differentiating gives $\mathrm{d}u=\frac{1}{5}\,\mathrm{d}x$, so $\mathrm{d}x=5\,\mathrm{d}u$.

Using the substitution and $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\tanh u=\sech^2 u$,

$$\begin{aligned}
\int\sech^2(\frac{1x}{5})\,\mathrm{d}x
&=5\int\sech^2 u\,\mathrm{d}u \\
&=5\tanh u+C \\
&=5\tanh(\frac{1x}{5})+C.
\end{aligned}$$

The argument is linear and the integrand is defined for every real $x$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=3x$. Then $\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{d}u$. When $x=1$, $u=3$; when $x=2$, $u=6$.

Using $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\sech u=-\sech u\tanh u$,

$$\begin{aligned}
\int_1^2\sech(3x)\tanh(3x)\,\mathrm{d}x
&=\frac{1}{3}\int_{3}^{6}\sech u\tanh u\,\mathrm{d}u \\
&=\frac{1}{3}[-\sech u]_{3}^{6} \\
&=\frac{1}{3}(\sech 3-\sech 6).
\end{aligned}$$

The integrand is continuous on $[1,2]$, and the result is positive because $\sech u$ decreases for $u>0$.
